faq.a: DVT presents with calf tenderness, swelling, and a positive Wells score; cellulitis shows erythema, warmth, and systemic signs of infection.
faq.q: How do I differentiate DVT from cellulitis clinically?

faq.q: When is anticoagulation contraindicated in leg problems?

exam: A 28‑year‑old with sickle cell disease presents with sudden calf pain and swelling – what investigations and immediate management steps are indicated? — Assess for DVT with Wells score, obtain CBC, start IV fluids and analgesia, consider anticoagulation if DVT likely.

A patient with HIV on antiretroviral therapy develops a warm, tender, erythematous leg swelling – how do you distinguish cellulitis from a deep‑vein thrombosis? — Look for systemic fever, skin breakdown, and use Wells score; ultrasound if available; treat cellulitis with antibiotics, DVT with anticoagulation.
You find a tense, painful calf after a road‑traffic injury – what is the next action and why? — Immediate fasciotomy is required to prevent muscle necrosis; delay increases risk of permanent loss.

A farmer presents with a chronic ulcer on the lower leg, non‑healing despite antibiotics – what tropical conditions should you consider? — Consider chronic venous insufficiency, leprosy, Buruli ulcer, and mycobacterial infection; obtain tissue biopsy if possible.

How does peripheral arterial disease present in a low‑resource setting and what bedside test helps? — Intermittent claudication, cool foot, absent pulses; ankle‑brachial index using a sphygmomanometer and Doppler if available.
Why are NSAIDs avoided in a patient with suspected DVT and renal impairment? — NSAIDs can worsen renal function and increase bleeding risk, compromising anticoagulation safety.
What are the red‑flag signs of a leg infection that require urgent referral? — Rapid progression, systemic toxicity, gas formation, necrotizing fasciitis signs; urgent surgical evaluation.
In a patient with bilateral leg edema, how do you prioritize investigations? — Check cardiac (BNP), renal (creatinine, albumin), and hepatic function; bedside ultrasound for ascites if available.
ai.title: Clinical Approach to the Leg
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: A systematic framework for evaluating leg complaints, integrating anatomy, common tropical pathologies, and limited-resource investigations to guide diagnosis and urgent management.

b: Key vessels: femoral artery → popliteal → anterior/posterior tibial.
Key nerves: femoral (anterior thigh), sciatic (posterior thigh), common peroneal (lateral leg), tibial (posterior leg).
sections.p: The leg comprises the thigh, knee, calf, ankle and foot, supplied by the femoral, popliteal and tibial vessels and innervated by the femoral, sciatic and peroneal nerves.

b: Acute unilateral swelling → consider DVT, cellulitis, trauma, compartment syndrome.
Chronic claudication → peripheral arterial disease, sickle cell vaso‑occlusion, peripheral neuropathy.
Bilateral edema → heart failure, nephrotic syndrome, hypoalbuminemia.
sections.p: When a patient presents with leg pain, swelling or dysfunction, categorize the problem by location (proximal vs distal), timing (acute vs chronic) and systemic clues (fever, trauma, sickle cell).

b: Identify “hard signs” of compartment syndrome: pain out of proportion, tense swelling, loss of pulses.
Look for “soft signs” of DVT: calf tenderness, swelling, Homan’s sign (pain on dorsiflexion).
Check for systemic infection: fever, leukocytosis, wound foul odor.
sections.p: In low‑resource East African hospitals, the most frequent leg emergencies are deep‑vein thrombosis (often related to HIV/TB treatment immobility), cellulitis from streptococci, sickle‑cell vaso‑occlusive crises, and tropical ulcers.

t.b: Confirms presence and extent of DVT; a positive study guides anticoagulation.
Estimates pre‑test probability of DVT; high score → treat empirically if ultrasound unavailable.
Detects leukocytosis for cellulitis or anemia in sickle‑cell crisis.
Assesses renal function before nephrotoxic drugs and identifies electrolyte shifts in sickle‑cell crisis.
Identifies fractures, osteomyelitis, or foreign bodies when plain radiography is the only imaging.

b: DVT: start low‑molecular‑weight heparin (or unfractionated heparin if monitoring possible); avoid NSAIDs that increase bleeding.
Cellulitis: give parenteral ampicillin‑sulbactam or ceftriaxone; avoid penicillin alone if MRSA risk is high.
Compartment syndrome: emergent fasciotomy; no delay for imaging.
Sickle‑cell crisis: give IV fluids, analgesics, and consider exchange transfusion if severe.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide analgesia, limb elevation and monitor for complications.

b: Palpate pulses proximally and distally; absent distal pulse suggests arterial occlusion.
Assess capillary refill; >2 seconds indicates poor perfusion.
Test sensation in the distribution of the peroneal and tibial nerves.
Check for a positive Homan’s sign but remember it is not specific.
sections.p: A focused leg exam can differentiate vascular, infectious and neurologic causes.

b: Assuming all leg swelling is due to heart failure; miss DVT or cellulitis.
Delaying fasciotomy for compartment syndrome because of lack of MRI.
Using only oral antibiotics for severe cellulitis in immunocompromised patients.
sections.p: Misinterpretation of swelling and pain often leads to delayed treatment.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of sensation or motor function
Pain out of proportion with tense swelling
